hops.afterHeading: The typical response: a burst at each end
hops.title: Feeling paper through a ballpoint pen
hops.text: Rest a fingertip on a sheet of printer paper, hold it perfectly still, and try to judge its texture. In lab tests with abrasive surfaces, differences in roughness became much harder to feel without sliding once the grains were smaller than about 100 micrometers, because a held press supplies no vibration. Now drag the tip of a capped ballpoint pen across the paper, then across your sleeve and the desk. Plastic has no nerves, yet each surface comes through clearly. Studies with handheld probes find that roughness felt this way is close to what the bare finger reports, carried up the barrel as vibration.

sources.citation: Hollins M, Risner SR (2000). Evidence for the duplex theory of tactile texture perception. Percept. Psychophys. 62(4):695-705.
Yoshioka T, Bensmaia SJ, Craig JC, Hsiao SS (2007). Texture perception through direct and indirect touch. Somatosens. Mot. Res. 24(1-2):53-70.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A hand lightly dragging a capped ballpoint pen across a denim sleeve and blank paper on a wooden desk.
image.caption: A still fingertip loses fine texture; a sliding pen carries it to your hand as vibration.

hops.afterHeading: Where force becomes current: Piezo2 in the axon
hops.title: Two patients born without working PIEZO2
hops.text: In 2016 a team at the National Institutes of Health described two patients, first seen at ages 18 and 8, born with inactivating variants in the PIEZO2 gene. Asked whether a 150 hertz vibration on the hairless skin of the hand was on or off, healthy volunteers were right 98 percent of the time. The patients managed 40 percent, no better than chance. They showed reduced vibration sensitivity on the forearm as well, and with eyes closed they could not walk and had profoundly impaired joint-position sense. Yet both sensed warmth and coolness much like controls, and both detected slow brushing on the forearm every time.

sources.citation: Chesler AT et al. (2016). The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation. N. Engl. J. Med. 375(14):1355-1364.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small metal vibrating probe on a wooden table beside a steaming teacup and an ice cube on a saucer.
image.caption: Both patients had severely impaired vibration and joint sense but still felt warmth and coolness much like controls.

hops.afterHeading: Vibration in the brain and in the wild
hops.title: How planthoppers led a biologist to elephant feet
hops.text: Before she studied elephants, biologist Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell spent hours in a soundproof chamber in Hawaii watching planthoppers, small insects that send calls through plant stems. She saw them call, freeze, press down on the stem and sometimes lift a leg. In 1992, at a watering hole in Namibia's Etosha National Park, she watched a herd of African elephants freeze with ears flat, rise onto their toes and sometimes raise one foot. Later studies of Asian elephants measured rumbles and stomps traveling through the ground at around 20 hertz, and found clusters of Pacinian corpuscles in their feet. Whether those corpuscles do the listening is still a proposal.

sources.citation: White T (2007). Caller ID in the wild: Elephants hear underground. Stanford Medicine News Center.
Ernst C (2007). Understanding Elephants. Malamalama, University of Hawaii System 32(2).
O'Connell-Rodwell CE, Arnason BT, Hart LA (2000). Seismic properties of Asian elephant vocalizations and locomotion. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 108(6):3066-3072.
